opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is that the human range in mathematics is much wider than people intuitively assume. There's an enormous distance between someone who can do competition-style problems well, which is roughly where we've seen the most dramatic recent progress, and a working research mathematician who can identify a fruitful open question, build the right definitions, and sustain an argument over dozens of pages. Then there's another big gap between a typical research mathematician and the very best people in the field. So even if systems are moving quickly, there's a lot of ground to cover.

The second reason is that the tasks that make up the upper part of that range differ in kind, not just in degree. Competition problems are short, self-contained, and have verifiable answers, which makes them well suited to the training approaches that have worked so well: reinforcement learning against checkable outcomes, lots of sampling, and search. Research mathematics involves long-horizon work where feedback is sparse. You might spend weeks on an approach before you know whether it's going anywhere. Much of the value lies in taste, in knowing which problems matter and which abstractions will pay off. Those are harder to provide training signal for, so I'd expect progress there to be slower and lumpier.

Third, there's a data and evaluation issue. We have relatively good benchmarks for the lower and middle parts of the range, and those benchmarks have been saturating quickly. As you push toward genuinely novel research, it becomes much harder to construct evaluations that are hard, uncontaminated, and verifiable. That slows down the feedback loop for developers, because it's harder to tell what's working.

Finally, if you look at how capabilities have historically scaled with compute, each step up in difficulty tends to require a substantial increase in training and inference resources. Compute is growing fast, but it's growing at a finite rate, and so are the algorithmic improvements that compound with it. When you put those together, crossing the remaining human range looks like something that plays out over several years rather than months.

None of this means it won't happen. I think it's quite likely that we'll see AI systems making meaningful contributions to research mathematics in the near term. But going from "useful collaborator on certain kinds of problems" to "matches or exceeds the best human mathematicians across the board" is a long stretch, and I'd be surprised if it were covered all at once.

r001.rationale: The response says compute requirements rise with task difficulty, but gives no estimate of three to four orders of magnitude or a comparison from basic arithmetic to near top-high-school ability.

r002.rationale: It contrasts short competition problems with research work and says research evaluations are harder to construct, but does not clearly state that verifying mathematical work itself becomes harder at research level than at high-school or undergraduate level.

r003.rationale: It describes research ability as identifying fruitful open questions and building useful definitions and abstractions, which captures generating ideas that enable further mathematical work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to recognize is that the human range in mathematics is just enormously wide. People tend to think of it as a fairly narrow band, but when you look at the gap between, say, a strong undergraduate who can do competition-style problems and someone like Terence Tao, that's not a small gap. That's many orders of magnitude in terms of the difficulty of the problems they can make progress on, the amount of background they can hold in their head, and the kind of taste and judgment they bring to picking what's worth working on in the first place.

And what we've seen so far is that AI has moved through the lower and middle part of that range fairly quickly. Competition math, olympiad problems, things that have a well-defined answer and a relatively short horizon, those have fallen. But those benchmarks saturate precisely because they're the easy end. Research mathematics is a very different kind of activity. It's open-ended, the horizons are long, you often don't know whether a problem is tractable, and progress depends on building up new concepts and machinery rather than cleverly applying known techniques.

So when I try to extrapolate, I look at a few things. One is the rate at which the horizon length of tasks these systems can do is growing, which has been doubling on the order of every several months. If you take research-level math as requiring horizons of months or years of focused effort, and you just run that trend forward, you get several years, not several months. The second is that the training signal gets much sparser as you move up. For competition problems you have clean verification, you can generate lots of problems, you can do reinforcement learning at scale. For genuine research, verification is harder, the problems are rarer, and the feedback loops are slower. That tends to slow things down.

And then the third thing is just that each time we've seen a capability jump, people have expected the next step to follow immediately, and it usually takes longer than the initial excitement suggests. I'm not saying it won't happen. I think it's quite likely AI will reach the top of the human range in mathematics. I'm just saying that the distance remaining is larger than the distance already covered, and the compute and algorithmic progress needed to close it is on the order of years rather than months.

r001.rationale: The response does not estimate the compute increase from basic arithmetic to near top-high-school mathematics.

r002.rationale: It says research math has harder verification than competition math, contrasting it with the clean verification available for competition problems.

r003.rationale: It describes research progress as requiring the creation of new concepts and machinery, rather than only applying known techniques.

astra-6.text:
I think the human range of mathematical ability is very wide. There’s a substantial gap between being able to solve problems that a typical person encounters, doing well on a math competition, and producing original research at the frontier. So reaching one of those milestones doesn’t necessarily mean that the others are immediately within reach.

In particular, research requires more than solving a well-specified problem. You have to identify useful questions, try approaches that might fail, and sustain a coherent line of reasoning over a long period. Those seem like capabilities that could take additional progress to develop reliably.

So my expectation is that moving through that whole range takes several years, even if progress remains quite rapid. But I wouldn’t put a great deal of confidence in the precise timing.

r001.rationale: The response gives no estimate of compute requirements or orders of magnitude.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss how the difficulty of verifying mathematical work changes by level.

r003.rationale: It mentions identifying useful questions and trying approaches, but does not clearly identify generating novel ideas that enable further mathematical work.

sol-6.1.text:
My expectation is that the human range of mathematical ability is quite wide. Getting from solving problems that a typical person can solve to doing competition mathematics is a substantial jump, and getting from there to producing important original research is another substantial jump. We tend to compress all of that into this one category of “human-level mathematics,” but it covers a lot of ground.

There’s also a difference between solving a well-specified problem and doing mathematical research. In research, you need to identify useful questions, choose promising approaches, and sustain a line of reasoning over a long period. Progress on benchmark problems is evidence of improving capabilities, but it doesn’t immediately establish that a system can do all of those things.

So I expect continued progress, potentially quite rapid progress, but I don’t think reaching one impressive milestone means we should expect the entire human range to be crossed immediately. Several more years seems plausible to me, though there’s a lot of uncertainty around that.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention compute or estimate the compute increase from basic arithmetic to near top-high-school mathematics.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes research from solving specified problems, but does not say that verifying mathematical work gets harder at research level.

r003.rationale: It mentions identifying useful questions and choosing approaches, but does not clearly identify generating novel ideas that enable further mathematical work.
